s4_subtitle: From a Stuttgart artisan workshop to the global benchmark for piano actions & hammerheads
s4_notes: Slide 4: Timeline of 140+ years of tradition (9 milestones). Key focus on Milestone 1 (1882: Founding in Stuttgart – The journey begins with piano actions; parallel to Carl Rönisch), Milestone 2 (1906: Dedicated hammerhead manufacturing – From Cristofori's leather-covered paper roll in 1700 to Renner's proprietary hammerhead production from 1906, which would later define the tone of every Steinway grand and establish a worldwide benchmark; image series featuring Cristofori, 1700 hammer action, historical action manufacturing and 1906 hammerhead presses), Milestone 3 (1911: Modernization & grand action manufacturing – Érard repetition action as cornerstone of modern grand piano playing; transition to Renner's first grand piano actions; Oscar Renner's industrial modernization with cutting-edge machinery, streamlined methods and transition from shaft drives to hundreds of individual electric motors; uniting all branches under one roof; image series featuring Sébastien Érard, 1808 Érard action and electrified workshop), Milestone 4 (1944: Air raid & rebuilding), Milestone 5 (1951/1952: Dr. Manfred Renner; 1955 return), Milestone 6 (1990: Fall of the Wall, historic turning point & survival – acquisition of Piano Union's action facility in Zeitz amidst pressure from Czech competitors to preserve largest customer Schimmel producing >40 pianos/day), Milestone 7 (2011: New facility in Gärtringen and modern manufacturing in Meuselwitz after relocating from Zeitz; consolidation across two core sites: Meuselwitz 6,800 m² and Gärtringen; image series featuring Gärtringen new facility and Meuselwitz bird's-eye view), Milestone 8 (2019: Steinway & Sons acquisition; tribute to Clemens von Arnim) and Milestone 9 (Preserving tradition, shaping future: Full consolidation of all operations in Meuselwitz following October 2025 launch with modern facility and new central filtration & extraction system; gratitude to Gärtringen workforce).

s16_notes: Slide 16: Comparison of the four Renner hammer moulding woods: Hornbeam and Maple are heavy hardwoods—Hornbeam is very demanding to season, yet ideal once properly dried; Maple can be more elastic, though irregular sugar deposits increase variance risks. Fine-grained, long-fibered American Walnut is the highest-grade tonewood: very light and ideal for a brilliant treble. Below: symmetrical profiles B, US, CSB and asymmetrical Form A.
s17_category: Part 3: Hammerhead Production • Acoustic Mass Scaling
s17_title: Optimal Hammerhead Weight Relative to String Weight
s17_subtitle: From ~15 g in the bass across the −1 g break step to 5 g in the treble: balancing contact time and string deflection
s17_phys_title: Crown Equilibrium: Contact Time τc ↔ String Deflection
s17_principle_txt: When string weight and hammerhead weight match, contact time τc and string deflection reach ideal equilibrium.
s17_notes: Slide 17: Equilibrium between string weight and hammerhead weight governs the balance between crown contact time τc and string deflection. The bass hammer starts around 15 g and is held high across the copper-wound section (~15–13 g) to drive heavy bass strings. At the break to plain steel strings, string mass drops sharply, requiring a deliberate 1 g hammer weight step (13 g → 12 g) before tapering down to 5 g at C8.

s27_category: Part 5: Voicing • Opening: Piano Tone Physics & Partials
s27_title: Partial Structure on A₁ (55 Hz): Felt Hardness & Strike Point
s27_subtitle: How felt elasticity and strike ratio (x₀ / L) shape partials H₁–H₁₂ in decibels (dB)
s27_str_title: Standing Wave A₁ (1,560 mm) & Node Cancellation
s27_notes: Slide 27 (Chapter 5 Opening: Voicing): Interactively demonstrate on bass note A₁ (55 Hz, speaking length L = 1,560 mm) how a piano tone is built from partials H₁–H₁₂. First show felt hardness: a softer, needled hammer lengthens contact time τc (~3.8 ms) and reduces upper partials in dB, whereas a harder crown (τc ~1.3 ms) boosts upper partials sharply. Next demonstrate the Young-Helmholtz strike-point law: striking near 1/8 L or 1/7 L suppresses dissonant partials (H₇ natural seventh, H₉ major second) at their nodes while preserving the singing major third H₅ (1/5 L).
s28_category: Part 5: Voicing • Spring Physics, Compaction Zones & Dynamic Limits
s28_title: The Hammerhead as a Complex Spring: From Cristofori to Zone Balance
s28_subtitle: How elasticity, 2:1 compaction (crown → ½ flank), and shoulder transition govern playable dynamics (pp–ff)
s28_curve_title: Change in Partial Structure (H1–H12 in dB)
s28_notes: Slide 28: Start with 1. Cristofori Roll (1700): the leather-covered hollow parchment cylinder uses circumferential ring tension with zero dead core mass for high restoring force and brief contact time τc. Then switch to 2. Renner Tension Spring: peak compaction sits at the crown, dropping to half (½) at the widest flank, anchored onto the hammer moulding by glue and rivet. Use the four 3-step controls to show that an overly hard crown/transition blocks pianissimo, while low elasticity or a locked shoulder prolongs τc and prevents fortissimo.

s29_subtitle: Always perpendicular to the wool fiber (⊥): from the 9:00–3:00 wedges to the elasticity stitch above the rivet

s29_z1_desc: Releases rigidity pre-underfelt, feeds f-wedge ↑ → open ff

s29_notes: Slide 29: Start with the golden rule: always align with the wrapped wool fiber course and work perpendicular to the fiber (⊥, 90°) in the upper 9:00–3:00 wedges so needles part fibers cleanly rather than severing them diagonally. Walk through: 1. Blue ff-wedge, 2. Green f-wedge, 3. Orange p-wedge, 4. Purple pp-wedge (≤ 2 mm between grooves). Then highlight 5. Above the Rivet → Toward Flank: using FEW but DEEP stitches angled from just above the rivet upward toward the flank boosts spring elasticity, shortens τc, and strengthens upper partials (H7–H12). 6. Red 12:00 core taboo.
s30_category: Part 5: Voicing • Geometry in the 3-String Unison Choir
s30_title: Crown & String Plane in 3-String Choirs: Phase & Cancellation
s30_subtitle: Even a 0.2 mm height or angle mismatch causes phase cancellation notches across partials H₁–H₁₂
s30_spec_title: Effect on H₁–H₁₂ (A₃ · 220 Hz): Phase Cancellation Notches in dB
s30_ctrl1_lbl: 1. Crown Angle Relative to String Plane
s30_notes: Aligning Hammerhead Crown & String Plane in 3-String Choirs (Slide 30): Before picking up a voicing needle, the hammer crown and the 3 unison strings must meet simultaneously in one exact plane. Even a 0.2–0.3 mm mismatch (from a tilted crown, unleveled agraffe/bridge strings, or a hollow crown) creates a fractional-millisecond delay Δt. On upper partials, this translates into 120°–180° phase shifts where wave crests meet wave troughs, collapsing the summed wave and carving deep comb-filter notches out of the harmonic spectrum.
s31_title: String Preparation: Hitch Pins, Bridge Pins & Agraffes
s31_subtitle: “Even the finest hammerhead can only bring out what is prepared in the instrument!”
s31_c1_title: Exact String Seating Before the First Needle Stitch
s31_c1_desc: Only firmly seated, level-aligned, and purely tuned string unisons allow an honest tonal diagnosis of the hammerhead.
s31_bullet_1: 1. Hitch Pins & Bearing: Clean bearing surfaces and check firm, tension-free string seating at the hitch pins.
s31_bullet_2: 2. Seat at Bridge Pins: Gently tap strings onto the bridge using a brass drift punch and light hammer to eliminate false beats.
s31_bullet_3: 3. Agraffes & String Plane: Level and space the 3 unison strings cleanly behind the agraffes using fine pliers.
s31_bullet_4: 4. Unison & Damper Check: Verify simultaneous hammer contact, clean damper seating, and 100% beatless unison tuning.
s31_fact: 🎵 Golden Rule: No needle can fix an unevenly seated or unlevel string unison!

s33_category: Part 5: Voicing • Post-Voicing Hardening & Hammer Weight Scaling
s33_title: Lacquer Dosing, Heat Ironing (max. 135 °C), Crown Finish & Weight
s33_subtitle: Interactive zone effects of lacquer hardeners, thermal smoothing, micro-polishing (≤ 15 µm) & register-specific hammer mass
s33_exp_title: Lacquer at the rivet reinforces the foundation and can lift felt tension
s33_exp_body: Applied in the rivet area, lacquer stiffens the lower hammer body and—depending on lacquer type—lifts felt tension while leaving flank elasticity untouched.
s33_exp_rule: ✓ Advantage: Located below the hammer moulding — the upper elastic impact arch stays protected.
s33_w_sub: Control via register-specific hammerhead weight (instead of over-hardening):
s33_w_detail_body: Higher hammerhead mass drives greater energy into heavy strings, boosting fundamental fullness and punch.
s33_caption_2: Thermostat-controlled voicing iron smooths and compacts the outer felt
s33_c2_title: Heat Ironing the Heads (up to max. 135 °C)
s33_c2_desc: Smoothing with a heated iron lays down raised fibers, compacts the outer zone, and lifts shell tension.
s33_bullet_3: Max. 135 °C Limit: Never iron hotter – higher heat damages wool keratin and natural lanolin.
s33_bullet_4: Smooth Motion: Glide evenly along the contour so internal spring elasticity stays intact.
s33_fact_2: 🌡️ Thermostat required: Max. 135 °C prevents fiber damage & scorching
s33_caption_3: Micro-abrasive down to 15 µm (left) or Braun Series 1 foil shaver (right)
s33_c3_desc: An ultra-smooth crown removes damping fuzz fibers and optimizes string-contact hardness without chemicals.
s33_bullet_5: Micro-Abrasive down to 15 µm (15 my): Polishes the crown mirror-smooth for crisp string contact.
s33_bullet_6: Braun Series 1 Foil Shaver: Standard foil shaver trims protruding fibers with zero felt loss.
s33_fact_3: ✨ Gentlest optimization: Pure tone & 100% preserved spring function
s33_notes: Slide 33: Interactively demonstrate lacquer impregnation: 1) In the rivet area, lacquer reinforces the foundation and, depending on the lacquer, can also lift felt tension. 2) Applied laterally above the hammer moulding, a light dose boosts high partials — whereas excess lacquer glues the connection to the flank and disrupts the spring function. 3) Strictly avoid lacquer directly on the crown (creates glassy, nasal hardness and risks permanent hammerhead damage). 4) Time factor: All applications above the hammer moulding compact further over playing time! 5) To increase fundamental fullness and projection, adjust hammerhead mass: increase weight from middle to bass (+m) and reduce weight toward the treble (-m). Alongside: heat ironing capped at max. 135 °C and ultra-fine crown finishing down to 15 µm or with a Braun Series 1 foil shaver.
